layout-reflow-supported.headline: Whether fixed and sticky chrome that swallows the reflowed viewport should be a normative failure rather than an advisory technique, and in what unit such a limit could be written.

positions.label: Sticky chrome makes pages non-functional
positions.detail: WayneEDick's original issue (wcag21#846, copied into #198 by michael-n-cooper) showed screenshots of content squished between a fixed header and footer, arguing the low-resolution assumption is a phone in portrait while a low-vision user is actually in landscape, and that non-collapsible vertical panes growing with zoom leave no usable space. StommePoes says these are simply non-functional pages: at 150% on a 12-inch laptop she gets about three lines of text, and she names Medium.com and news sites as the worst offenders, failing them under text-resize in her own audits. mraccess77 adds breakages with the same cause — hover content that appears off-screen and vanishes when you scroll to it, snap scrolling that jumps past content you are trying to reach at zoom, and scroll jacking that takes away ctrl plus mouse wheel. All three treat the fix as cheap and known — WayneEDick's three techniques are switch fixed to static at low resolution, replace the bar with a control limited to 10% of the screen, or make it collapsible, and StommePoes adds that developers already write width-based media queries, so a height-based one in ems can simply drop the stickiness, since the sticky content is usually the site name or social buttons.

positions.label: A ratio threshold, worded 'down to'
positions.detail: patrickhlauke would support a percentage or ratio rule — roughly, sticky and fixed elements not covering more than a third of the visible viewport — with the understanding doc requiring testing in both portrait and landscape, down to 320 CSS px width and 256 CSS px height. He insists on "down to" rather than mandating that exact viewport dimension, because otherwise the requirement is pointless. StommePoes agrees, citing content that passed at 400% on a 1280 px viewport but broke around 250% when a media query did not fire, leaving the user to choose between 175% (too small) and 300% (larger than needed); she also reports that showing designers sticky elements eating a quarter to a half of viewport height draws no pushback, because they find it ridiculous too.

positions.label: Measurement is the blocker
positions.detail: Sticky headers create reading viewports that are too short, but mraccess77 doubts the group can reach consensus on what height is acceptable: is the metric percent of viewport height, or the number of lines of text that fit? Full coverage is clearly a failure, but two or three visible lines forcing the user to read through a slot is harder to draw a line around. He notes the LVTF concluded these issues were too challenging for WCAG 2.2's framework and belonged in Silver, and that the working group's impression is that low-vision issues are already solved — leaving him unsure which spec is the right home. alastc was more optimistic, suggesting a limit could build on reflow's existing 256 px minimum height and tie in with device orientation.

positions.label: Authors cannot be held to device density
positions.detail: PAFaieta opened #156 asking that the standard name a baseline native viewport resolution and DPI, or a baseline minimum magnification such as 200% as a satisfactory technique, on the grounds that vague language invites compliance arguments. patrickhlauke answered that CSS px is already density-independent and that authors cannot predict or test the physical resolution and dimensions users run — a person on a physically small monitor at very high resolution has chosen that, and adapting the device is their call, not the author's. alastc added that WCAG 3 deliberately avoids technology-specific language at the provision level and expects metrics to live in technology-specific methods, and asked for concrete ground-level examples of the "liberties" being taken; PAFaieta left the thread without supplying them.

positions.label: Layouts set in px are the root cause
positions.detail: chaals set font-size to 64px in Safari and browsed roughly 100 pages: news sites were generally unusable (abc.net.au the least bad), search engines were terrible, whitehouse.gov and un.org worked reasonably, and idealista was the one usable shopping site. He reports that pretty much every serious problem traced to layouts set in pixels — most commonly line-heights derived from the screen's pixel width and far below 64px, then large text squeezed into too-small boxes. His proposal is to trigger breakpoints on character counts rather than screen width in px, and to express any measure larger than half the expected font-size in rem, with layouts expected to work between 4px and 72px (about 1.5mm to 25mm). graphic-designer (#642) argues the same conclusion from user autonomy: px ignores a user's configured root font size, so a px-based architecture is rigid by construction while rem lets the layout breathe.

positions.label: CSS px is the right unit; zoom beats text-only sizing
positions.detail: Responding to #642, alastc says WCAG 3 has no mention of 16px, that its only CSS px requirements are text resizing to 200% of the platform default body size and text reflow at 320 CSS px, and that CSS px is itself relative to an assumed viewing distance and translates to platforms that have no rem. He argues browser zoom is the default, easier-to-find setting that persists across sites, that text-only sizing breaks text out of layouts, and that sizing the whole layout in rem just re-invents zoom; his draft response would close the issue without changing provisions. Myndex says the CSS px is defined as a unit of visual angle, which is what vision science uses, while rem has no fixed relation to it, and that Chrome is the only major browser he knows with an independent default font size setting. GreggVan says rem says nothing about how large something is, so an accessibility minimum cannot be written in it, and that CSS px values are cited in standards only as minimums. chaals, after testing, agreed zoom works better than increased text size on most sites, while still seeing a use case for text-only sizing to keep headings and images from becoming unworkable.

positions.label: Reflow itself is the barrier
positions.detail: An emailed objection from an unnamed sender, which alastc posted as #664, argues that forcing a 320 px mobile-style layout on a desktop display at 400% zoom increases cognitive load for older users by hiding familiar navigation and breaking established mental models. It claims this breaks complex interfaces such as legal document portals, preventing citizens from accessing documents, and characterises the mobile-first target as favouring the ecosystems of major W3C corporate members. The request is for a Desktop-Preservation Mode or a reduced requirement — 200% — that does not trigger a full layout change. Nobody has replied.

agreed: Fixed headers, footers and non-collapsible side panes that stay put under zoom render pages non-functional. StommePoes's flat "absolutely" to WayneEDick's question went unchallenged in eight years of thread.

The fixes are not technically hard — un-fixing via vertical media queries, collapsing, or allowing dismissal after reading — and no one argued they are expensive. StommePoes notes developers do not think of them but implement them readily once shown.
open: Whether any limit on sticky and fixed chrome becomes normative in WCAG 3 or stays advisory as C34. alastc said in 2019 it needed a couple of people to work on it; mraccess77 offered to take something on for 2.2 if the issue had a solution there, but nothing further came of it in the thread.

How to measure it at all — mraccess77 asked whether it should be percent of viewport height or number of readable lines. patrickhlauke and StommePoes favoured a percentage or ratio (roughly a third, or a quarter, of the viewport), and StommePoes also floated a lines-visible measure drawn from caption research; nothing was settled.
What alastc's 2019 idea of building on the 256 px reflow minimum height and tying it to device orientation actually was. jake-abma asked him to lift the veil and got no reply.

Whether #198 belongs in WCAG 3 at all. scottaohara asked whether it should have been transferred rather than cloned, since his reflow understanding-doc PR would likely have addressed it in WCAG 2; cwadamsoforacle said the chairs made a blanket decision to move wcag.next issues into WCAG 3 and would review it with alastc. No further word in the thread.
Whether the 400% / 320 CSS px reflow target itself harms desktop users who do not want a mobile layout (#664), which has drawn no response.

chaals's proposed workable range of 4px to 72px is explicitly a guess; he asks for systematic research across more scripts, screen sizes, font sizes and content types, noting he covered only a handful of Chinese and Russian pages and nothing in Japanese or Arabic.

Whether #156's request for a native-resolution, DPI or baseline-magnification reference needs any provision. patrickhlauke argued CSS px is density-independent and alastc that metrics belong in technology-specific methods; PAFaieta disputed the first point and then left the thread, so neither view was tested further.
layout-reflow-supported.note: #198 dates from 2018 (transferred from wcag21#846) and is still open with no normative outcome. #642 turned procedural: rachaelbradley intervened as chair to say GitHub discussion is between individuals, that a formal response on units may take months, and to ask for polite professionalism — after graphic-designer filed a DMCA counter-notification over the Google Drive copy of his full proposal, published mirrored "audit log" copies, and reported the thread to Open Web Advocacy and Open Digital Design over other participants deleting their own comments. alastc has drafted a response closing #642 without changing any provision, but it has not been through the AG group. #664 arrived by email and has no comments at all.

relationships-detectable.headline: Whether "relationships detectable" is purely a programmatic requirement, and how to bound it — the two substantive threads behind it are both stalled proposals inherited from WCAG 2.x, one on element nesting and one on visual label proximity.

positions.label: A new provision for role nesting
positions.detail: cstrobbe's proposal in #166 would require that elements used with their native roles be nested according to the content models in their specifications, plus a fourth clause barring links, interactive elements and keyboard-focusable elements as descendants of links. He worked through seventeen code examples (numbered 1 to 16, then 19) showing where a syntax reading of 4.1.1, a validation reading, and the proposal each land — button wrapping an anchor, li inside a div inside a ul, p as a sibling of li, h2 wrapping p. JAWS-test called it exactly what was needed and asked that it also cover ARIA and PDF tags, noting that correct nesting is what lets a screen reader report that a table has 3 columns and 2 rows and that you are in column 2, row 1. JAWS-test cited EN 301 549 clause 11.5.2.9 and Section 508 502.3.7, both of which already require parent-child relationships to be programmatically determinable.

positions.label: Fix or retire 4.1.1 instead of adding a provision
positions.detail: patrickhlauke would rather see 4.1.1 updated normatively in a backwards-compatible way than patch around a poorly interpreted criterion, warning of weird overlaps where one SC is a stricter special case of another. yatil proposes extending 4.1.1 to "markup languages and associated extensions as they relate to accessibility features" and dropping the well-formedness framing from the Understanding document, or alternatively removing 4.1.1 entirely per w3c/wcag#2676. scottaohara agrees: use 4.1.1 for what people think it is for, unless "elements are nested according to their specifications" does not actually mean that. patrickhlauke also argues the singling out of links is arbitrary, since buttons and other controls have the same problem.

positions.label: Do not reinterpret 4.1.1 after the fact
positions.detail: bruce-usab says it is bad to retcon a standard and refuses scottaohara's "use 4.1.1 for what people think it's for" framing; GreggVan agrees and adds that 4.1.1 should be clarified to mean what the working group meant when it was written, not what people later want it to mean. bruce-usab separately notes the proposal arrived too late for WCAG 2.2. cstrobbe's own reply is that the intents differ: 4.1.1 is about a user agent building an unambiguous parse tree, while his proposal is about name, role, state and value being exposed unambiguously through an accessibility API, which puts it closer to 4.1.2.

positions.label: Measure the label gap
positions.detail: detlevhfischer's #194 proposal caps the gap between a label and the element it labels at twice the smaller of the labelled element's width or height, illustrated with a 16 px-tall field passing at a 32 px gap and failing at 33 px. He later revised it to four times the smaller dimension of the label itself, to escape the problem that the original formula breaks for textarea. mraccess77 defends the need against demands for evidence, pointing out that the SC 3.3.2 Understanding document said in 2008 that labels close to their field help screen-magnifier users, that G162 already exists, and citing Nielsen Norman Group material on proximity and form white space; to the argument that proximity gaps are a common pattern he answers that "because something is a common pattern doesn't mean it's a correct pattern."

positions.label: The gap metric breaks real designs and lacks evidence
positions.detail: jake-abma checked with designers and reported that almost all current forms would fail and that the calculation is too prescriptive for design aesthetics, and that the measurement scheme — four times, three times, widths, heights, mixed elements — is too complicated for designers, developers and testers alike. awkawk points to the very common pattern of left-aligned labels against aligned fields, where varying label length forces varying gaps, and says disallowing a common pattern requires clear evidence. alastc notes the proposal would fail the GOV.UK Design System text input with hint text, and asks what happens when an error message is inserted. patrickhlauke finds the loophole immediately: a designer could make fields excessively tall purely to buy leeway to push the label further away, defeating the point while passing; he also asks for hard proof that larger gaps harm particular users rather than the working group making things up. detlevhfischer concedes the exception list grows until the original requirement is lost, and that focusing on label-to-control catches only a subset of the proximity problems he has seen in low-vision user testing.

positions.label: The requirement is unbounded as written
positions.detail: In #451 GreggVan argues that if a relationship is not presented to anybody, it is unclear what the requirement is getting at, and that without scoping there are a million ways elements can be related and all of them would have to be conveyed programmatically; he proposes narrowing it to "when relationships of meaning between elements are presented visually, they are also conveyed programmatically." giacomo-petri opened the issue acknowledging the tests are incomplete and that the requirement must either gain sufficient tests or state its applicability clearly. adampage's specific gaps are error messages and help text for form controls, and tables with headers, bodies, footers, data cells and header cells — questions that arise precisely because the written tests are so narrow.

agreed: Proximity of a label to its control genuinely matters for low-vision and magnifier users; awkawk, the main sceptic on #194, states outright that he does not dispute the concept and that the challenge is only deciding how close is close enough so it can be tested. patrickhlauke still asked for hard proof that larger gaps can be a problem for particular users, so the evidence base itself remained in question.

A whole class of parent-child relationships is not expressible as element nesting at all — JAWS-test's list of aria-owns, radio buttons grouped by the name attribute, and aria-level on treegrids drew no rebuttal, and cstrobbe conceded the requirement should be framed around what reaches the accessibility API and not only around nesting.
open: Whether the provision stays limited to programmatic relationships or additionally requires visually clear ones. adampage raised it on #194 against the current draft text; patrickhlauke's objection is that defining how to represent something "clearly" in visual terms lands you in arbitrary graphic design statements.
Whether the requirement should apply only where a relationship is presented visually, per GreggVan's proposed rewording in #451.
What the tests must cover: error messages and help text for form controls, and table headers, bodies, footers and cells — adampage's list, carried into #451 by giacomo-petri.

What artefact is evaluated — source code, DOM or accessibility tree. JAWS-test raised this on #166: source often has no bearing after JS and CSS, while DOM and accessibility tree reflect browser repair that is not consistent across browsers, which is why 4.1.1 existed in the first place.

Whether roles overridden by ARIA are in scope, and how to word that technology-independently. This is cstrobbe's own question on #166. JAWS-test answered it in favour, arguing ARIA is exactly where the problems are, since it is widely misused, hard to validate and not consistently repaired by browsers, and suggested wording along the lines of EN 301 549 and Section 508; cstrobbe said he would submit a suggestion covering explicitly assigned roles, but never posted it.

Whether any testable proximity metric is achievable at all. jake-abma and patrickhlauke floated a reflow-style alternative — label and input both at least partly visible in a 320 CSS px viewport — and jake-abma noted it leaves desktop zoom-tool users, where the label is simply too far right, unaddressed.

Whether a programmatic relationship should serve as an escape hatch from a visual proximity requirement. alastc proposed it; patrickhlauke called it a cop-out that shifts the burden to user agents and makes the provision redundant, since programmatic association is already required by 1.3.1 and in most cases 4.1.2.
relationships-detectable.note: Both substantive threads are inherited and largely dormant. #194 was opened in 2019 as a WCAG 2.2 proposal, had its real debate over two weeks in March and April 2019, drew one comment in 2022 from anevins12 that went unanswered, then sat untouched until adampage reopened the question in May 2026 against the WCAG 3 draft text. #166 dates from 2022 and its last exchange is bruce-usab and GreggVan on retconning, with cstrobbe's promised rewording never posted. #271 is alastc's requirement-tracking stub listing five requirements and a Google doc link, with no discussion at all.

decorative-images-hidden.headline: Whether WCAG 3's "decorative" has quietly widened WCAG 2's "pure decoration" into a loophole, and whether the fix is a tighter definition, a second tier of decorative images that may carry alt text, or abolishing the exemption entirely.

positions.label: Abolish the exemption
positions.detail: The starting point is ericwbailey's framing in #238 that an abled content author deciding what counts as decorative removes agency from the person using assistive technology, with a case he met in the wild (photos of amenities for luxury housing classed as decorative even though they communicate the benefit of living there); ericwbailey himself did not call for abolition, and suggested tempering the point by testing with the intended audience. brett-oppegaard goes further in #369 — a designer told him a stock photo of a diverse group reading books in front of a university building was decorative and therefore not legally required to be described, and he has heard the same claim made about portrait photos of organizational leaders. His argument is that visual designers always have the option not to include an image, so every included image has a rhetorical purpose; that a screen reader user can skip alt text with a single keypress, so the audience should decide, not millions of decentralized, busy, often untrained site managers; and that the loophole is why Instagram alone emits 70,000 mostly undescribed images a minute. He also wants the term "alt text" retired in favour of static Audio Description, which he argues separately in #371 (see image-alternatives-available). charleshalldesign takes the same line in #878, proposing to retire the concept completely on the grounds that all images convey information, and that an image next to text, in a control or not, supplements the text rather than duplicating it.

positions.label: Over-description is its own barrier
positions.detail: TestPartners reports content creators over-compensating with literal descriptions of decorative images running to several sentences and as much as 50 words, which a screen reader user must sit through a large proportion of before concluding it is fluff they did not need; he puts community opinion at roughly 50:50 and says a substantial majority should exist before anything changes. He half-seriously proposed a CSS prefers-reduced-fluff property as the only way to satisfy both camps, and rejects the premise that undescribed decorative images discriminate — you may as well argue that hanging wallpaper discriminates against people who cannot see it. patrickhlauke's reductio in #238 is that if every non-text piece of information must be conveyed, authors would have to describe colour and sizing choices and ultimately the entire CSS of the page, so a pragmatic and admittedly subjective cut-off is unavoidable; he adds that where a flourish exists to convey a mood, prose carrying the same tone can already be an acceptable alternative. bruce-usab makes the placement argument against Myndex's paisley example: the fact that paisley patterns descend from Jacquard-loom punch cards is compelling trivia that belongs in the footer or on an About page available to everyone, not buried in an alt attribute forced only on screen reader users.

positions.label: Hold the WCAG 2 line
positions.detail: yatil's objection in #369 is that WCAG has said "pure decoration" since 2008 and merely being decorative never qualified for the exception — WCAG comes from the era of image-rendered container shadows and image-replacement headings, and most genuinely pure decoration can now be done in CSS. He argues the draft's test, whether removing the image would impact how people understand the page, is far too low a bar: under it a portrait in a staff index is decorative and so is a news article photo, and neither "impact" nor "understand" is defined. lauracarlson opened #238 on the narrower charge that "Decorative Images" is broader than "Pure Decoration" and that conflating them is a mistake; her specific target is the Method's "Illustrative of adjacent text but not contributing information (eye-candy)" line, and she proposed renaming "Decorative" to "Purely Decorative" throughout. She calls null alt a hangover from the spacer-gif era; bruce-usab agrees null alt is overused, though he says his own sampling shows missing alt and low-information alt attempted as textual equivalence remain the bigger problems, while allowing this may be sampling bias. In #878 yatil asks the group to stick to WCAG 2's pure decoration definition, since both standards will be used in parallel for years, and says the linked-card examples raised there fall under the Controls, Input exception instead.

positions.label: Two tiers, with alt optional on the softer one
positions.detail: MakotoUeki opened #466 proposing an explicit split: purely decorative images (an icon alongside text, a thumbnail inside a link) need no text alternative and should have no accessible name, while decorative images (a photo, an illustration) may usefully carry one as a best practice. The user need he cites is a person who lost their sight later in life and wants the description in order to picture the image, and his position in #238 is that the user, not the author, should decide whether something is meaningless. fstrr points at a ready-made middle category: the HTML spec's ancillary images, where an image is neither purely decorative nor entirely redundant with the text, the alt attribute must be present, its value may be the empty string or a textual representation, and it must not be empty when the image has a caption.

positions.label: One category, defined properly
positions.detail: grace-snow's reply in #466 is that if an image adds meaning it is not decorative at all, so naming a class of "decorative" images that do need alternative text is highly likely to confuse; whether a photo or illustration is decorative depends on the surrounding content and context, not on the image type. Finnberrys agrees and offers the substitution test she applies: a swirly line at the bottom of a page could be swapped for a wiggly rainbow line with no effect on content, whereas a photo of her dog on a page about assistance dogs could not be swapped for a unicorn without becoming confusing and weird. sydneycolemanfromgoogle filed the same objection independently in #518 — the distinction is not useful without a clear and mostly objective means of telling the two apart.

positions.label: The gap is in user agents, not author judgement
positions.detail: mraccess77 reports that Internet Explorer's exposure of alt as a tooltip let him learn things about images he could not distinguish visually — essentially audio description for the web, the nuances low-vision users miss — and notes that captions today are available to everyone rather than only to deaf users, while accessible name and description are not. Myndex makes the adoption argument: alt text is effectively unreachable outside screen reader use, and if it surfaced through a standard user-agent affordance it would serve people with prosopagnosia or other cognitive and contextual needs, reader mode, and failed image loads, and the broader demand would drive adoption. bruce-usab counters from history that IE's tooltip behaviour is precisely what trained authors to write tooltips into alt for years, that the TITLE attribute only partly separated them, and that the practice only corrected when touch UIs removed the tooltip, though after mraccess77's reply he allowed he was probably overstating the harm and that some human-written alt is almost always better than none. Myndex also flags that CSS background images accept no alt text at all, which he treats as a missing platform property rather than an author failing.

positions.label: Redefine the threshold, and the verbosity cost
positions.who: alastc, lauracarlson, MakotoUeki, mraccess77, patrickhlauke, LJWatson, vavroom
positions.detail: #878, opened by alastc on 2026-09-29 after vavroom's article on retiring decorative images, is where the definition argument now runs. alastc floated redefining it as not contributing to the information, functionality, meaning, mood or context, then asked whether not relied on would be better after patrickhlauke noted that mood can also be carried by the tone of the text. lauracarlson revived her purely decorative proposal, with a definition excluding anything that provides meaning, context, mood or user understanding, and with alastc reframed generic card images and linked thumbnails as duplicative rather than decorative. MakotoUeki, facilitating the subgroup, said it will not stick to WCAG 2's definitions and wants to gather concrete examples. On verbosity, alastc reports screen reader users split between wanting descriptions and wanting to get on with the task; patrickhlauke warns that requiring alternatives for most images will produce LLM-generated descriptions and distinguishes an alternative from an on-demand description; mraccess77 argues that alt on every image without importance metadata, such as an aria-important attribute, would leave users no way to control verbosity, and cites invisible email tracking images as genuinely ignorable. LJWatson and vavroom answer that content that is present can be skipped while absent content cannot.

agreed: Null alt is overused and "decorative" gets stretched to cover images that inform — bruce-usab and MakotoUeki both concede this to lauracarlson, though TestPartners, and in #878 alastc and mraccess77, warn about the verbosity cost of describing more images.

Several participants treat applying the exemption as subjective: TestPartners says there is no right answer and patrickhlauke describes a pragmatic, subjective cut-off. jake-abma's example is the WCAG 2.1 CSS-fitting-images working example, which shipped with alt="" and which he says mraccess77 wanted described during sanity-checking; jake-abma's conclusion was that a judgement call may not be the best approach and that it comes down to the user.

The overlap with Images detectable that scottaohara raised via #357 — how can an image be hidden and detectable at once, and where do CSS background images land — was resolved editorially; scottaohara accepted the reworked text in the Jan 5 draft preview and adampage closed the issue on 2026-04-01.
open: Whether "decorative" should be one category or two. MakotoUeki (#466) wants the split; grace-snow, Finnberrys and sydneycolemanfromgoogle want one term defined well. adampage marked sydneycolemanfromgoogle's #518 as a duplicate of #466 rather than answering it (the issue is still open), and the question is now argued mainly in #878, where lauracarlson and MakotoUeki back purely decorative, vavroom is undecided on wording, charleshalldesign wants no category at all, and yatil wants WCAG 2's pure decoration kept.

Whether the exemption should exist at all. brett-oppegaard's #369 poses it as five direct questions — what the exemption is for and whether WCAG serves designers or the audience, how blind people can be included in societal discussions if excluded from these elements, what the downside of removing it is, and whether the old page-loading rationale still applies, plus a demand that, if kept, WCAG define "decorative" in a legal sense — and none has been answered on the record.

Whether the author or the user decides an image is meaningless. ericwbailey, MakotoUeki and jake-abma all land on the user, as do LJWatson and vavroom in #878. Mechanisms have been floated but not pursued: TestPartners' prefers-reduced-fluff property, mraccess77's importance metadata, and patrickhlauke's and yatil's on-demand generic descriptions carried with the image.

What research supports widening "pure decoration" to "decorative". lauracarlson asked for the data in January 2022 and again in her follow-up; jake-abma's answer was that data is not always available and the judgement is inherently subjective. In #878 lauracarlson cited TetraLogical research on images as cognitive anchors for neurodivergent users and user testing summarized by David MacDonald; no other study has been cited.
Whether CSS background images can carry alternatives at all — Myndex raised it in #238 and it is the same hole scottaohara found from the Images detectable side in #357.

Whether authors should be describing emotionally rich images and, if so, how. lauracarlson pointed at Léonie Watson's and Jake Archibald's writing on emotion in text descriptions; #238 did not take it up, though LJWatson pointed to the same writing in #878.

Whether yatil's asymmetry argument holds: information that is present can be skipped by the user, information that was never provided cannot be recovered. LJWatson and vavroom make the same point in #878; mraccess77 counters that without metadata the user has no way to know what to skip.

Whether the drafted test procedure gets fixed. grace-snow (#573) shows it is written only for img, ignores svg and role="img", omits that role="img" must be absent from a decorative image, and omits aria-hidden="true" as a technique; JasonAment (#607) shows the first procedure's help text duplicates a condition of the second; janBeniaminKwiek (#614) asks that "add no information to the content" become "add no information or functionality". None of these has drawn a reply.

The self-contradiction WilcoFiers raises in #495 is unanswered: if content is what is communicated to the user and a decorative image is by definition not that, then a decorative image cannot have programmatically determinable properties and therefore cannot be programmatically hidden. He recommends reverting to WCAG 2.0's definition of programmatically determined, which lacks the word "important".

Whether programmatically hidden is the right term at all: mcking65 (#884) says it is generally understood to mean hidden from every user, as with display:none or the hidden attribute, and proposes WCAG 2.2-style wording such as ignored by, or hidden from, assistive technology. MakotoUeki replied that the subgroup will address it when its review begins, as early as the first half of next year.
decorative-images-hidden.note: This provision's history runs in disconnected phases. #238 was argued out in January 2022, bruce-usab took the concrete fix to EOWG as a pull request against the WAI tutorial (wai-tutorials#635), it was considered and declined, and he asked lauracarlson to close; she declined in September 2022 on the grounds that the full AG Working Group should consider it and that WCAG 3 should not inherit the tutorial's examples. The issue then sat untouched for three years until brett-oppegaard revived the argument in September 2025. Several of the more consequential recent filings — #495, #573, #607, #614 — are single unanswered comments, so the quality of the current draft text has had far less scrutiny than the definition has. The definition argument restarted in #878, opened by alastc on 2026-09-29, which drew 34 comments in five days and is unresolved; #884 (mcking65, 2026-10-02) separately challenges the term programmatically hidden. Note also that brett-oppegaard participates by email, so his comments arrive with quoted reply chains attached.

interactive-element-names-available.headline: Whether the visual gap between a label and the control it labels can be written as a testable numeric requirement at all — argued out on one 2019 thread while the issues about accessible names themselves have drawn a single reply between them.

positions.label: Iterate until the gap is measurable
positions.detail: Proposed "Label gaps" in #194: when one element acts as a label of another, the gap between them is no larger than twice the smaller of the labelled element's width or height, measurable with a browser ruler or a script comparing absolute positions. When textareas broke that formula he reworked it to four times the smaller dimension of the label itself, so an icon or short text label sets the budget rather than a large field. He cites repeated findings in his own user testing with low vision users — drop-down menus on accessuse.eu and the incobs tablet tests — while conceding the label-to-control pair catches only a subset of the proximity problem, and that the exception list may grow until the requirement is lost, as happened with target size.

positions.label: Any arbitrary line will be gamed and cannot be justified
positions.detail: Found the loophole immediately: a designer could make fields unnecessarily tall purely to buy leeway to push the label further away, conforming while defeating the point for low vision users. detlevhfischer answered "not likely to happen"; patrickhlauke replied that creative interpretations of normative text to do the minimum necessary to pass are routine. His broader position is that layout and design questions resist rigid binary pass/fail rules, that Apple's own iOS guidance is couched as could and should and Apple ignores it freely, and that this belongs in a non-normative best-practice note or at AAA rather than as a hard requirement. He also asked that the measurement drop mm for px to avoid reopening the CSS-versus-physical-units confusion, which detlevhfischer did immediately.

positions.label: Do not fail a common pattern without evidence
positions.detail: awkawk points to left-aligned label columns with aligned fields, where varying label lengths necessarily produce varying gaps, and argues this is common enough that the working group needs clear evidence before proposing a criterion against it — this is not an absolute like page title or programmatic label association. He wants the goal stated first: at what magnification must the user see the full label and the full input, or the full label and part of the input, and what happens when the label is long. jake-abma checked with designers and reported back that almost all current forms would fail the proposed calculation, which he called too prescriptive for design aesthetics, and later that mixed 3x and 4x width-or-height measurements are simply too complicated for designers, developers and testers.

positions.label: Commonality is not correctness, and the evidence already exists
positions.detail: Answers awkawk that clear evidence only ever comes from research, and the group has a chicken-and-egg problem when practitioner experience outruns formal study. Cites the Understanding document for SC 3.3.2, which stated in 2008 that labels in close proximity assist screen magnifier users because field and label are more likely to be visible within the magnified area, plus technique G162 and two Nielsen Norman Group articles on closeness of actions to objects and form white space. Turns the evidence demand back on existing criteria by questioning whether page titles are still demonstrably useful when browsers truncate or hide them. Calls awkawk's own screenshot a prime example of the problem: a common pattern is not thereby a correct one.

positions.label: Reframe it as a viewport test instead of a ruler
positions.detail: patrickhlauke suggested a minimum built on reflow rather than ratios: the related element must be at least partly present in the viewport even at 320 CSS px width. jake-abma picked this up as the direction most likely to work — label and input visible in a 320 CSS px viewport at the same time, easy to test, with exceptions. He also supplied its limits: whether the label is visible depends on how far you have scrolled, something can be inside the viewport and still too far to read, and desktop zoom tools push the label off to the right and force horizontal scrolling, so the desktop case stays unsolved.

positions.label: Widen the scope, or leave the gap to AT
positions.detail: alastc showed the formula failing a usable pattern — the GOV.UK Design System text input with hint text between label and field, and again when an error message is inserted — then proposed folding associated information into the definition of label, and a looser framing that two related things must be close to each other unless there is a programmatic relationship, with gestalt principles consulted for what close means. He intended the escape hatch to leave room for a future user agent that draws an arrow or indicator, and suggested the COGA task force's design guidance as the better home. patrickhlauke rejected both halves: if the requirement is visual then a programmatic relationship is irrelevant to a user who is not running AT that exposes it, shifting the burden to user agents is a cop-out, and since programmatic association is already required by 1.3.1 and usually 4.1.2, a criterion satisfiable by passing those is redundant. jake-abma agreed on widening, arguing all name-value pairs and many other related pairs deserve the same treatment.

positions.label: Split the visual label from the programmatic name
positions.detail: In #890 (October 2026) mcking65 proposes removing the programmatically available requirement from this provision, rewording it as "Names (including labels) that identify the purpose of the interactive element are visually persistent", and moving programmatic names into Roles, values, states, properties available, reworded so those attributes are "reliably" programmatically determinable. His grounds are that visual and API testing are separate processes, often by separate testers, and that bugs are easier to route when a provision clearly concerns visual design or code. GreggVan objects that "reliably" cannot be defined to mean matching the visible label and is not an objective term, that names do not include labels — labels have meant what is visible and names what is programmatically determinable — and that the name often should say more than the label, as with ON/OFF buttons whose association is visually obvious. He asks the group to start from desired outcomes for users without vision, with good vision and with low vision (and cognitive needs if not covered elsewhere), then decide whether this is one requirement or two.

agreed: That proximity between related information matters for low vision and magnifier users was never disputed — awkawk states plainly that the concept is clear and everyone can see how it impacts people, and mraccess77 cited the 2008 SC 3.3.2 Understanding text and G162, though patrickhlauke later still asked for hard proof that larger gaps are a problem for particular users. The disagreement is entirely about whether "how close is close enough" can be drawn as a line.

The problem is not specific to form labels. patrickhlauke asked whether any two insufficiently close related elements cause the same problem for low vision and zoom users, and jake-abma agreed, extending it to all name-value pairs — neither treated label-and-input as the natural boundary, though patrickhlauke added that taken to its conclusion this would mean mandating whitespace and layout for everything on a page, which he said would not fly.
Measurement should use CSS px, not mm; detlevhfischer changed the draft on patrickhlauke's first comment.
The first formula does not survive real components — textareas break it (detlevhfischer), and hint text or an inserted error message between label and field break it (alastc). Both were conceded.
open: Whether "Relationships detectable" must stay limited to programmatic relationships or could additionally require visually clear ones — adampage raised this in #194 in May 2026, pointing at #175; patrickhlauke's only reply was that defining how to represent something visually "clearly" lands you in arbitrary graphic design statements. Nothing else followed.

tallneil's #93: whether the provision should require labels to remain visible "at all times" or "in all states" so the label survives after a value is set, and whether it should say explicitly that a placeholder attribute or the first option in a select are not sufficient substitutes for a label. Opened June 2024, no replies.

mraccess77's #184: whether a button's accessible name must carry its context — an "Add" button beside a person's name is visually related but not programmatically — and whether that is a failure of 1.3.1, of 2.4.6, or of neither. He notes buttons are unlike links in that they rarely sit inside a sentence and may act on a whole group of fields, so the link-context reasoning does not transfer, and asks where the line for buttons is drawn. Deferred from w3c/wcag#168 in 2016, still no replies.
What magnification level any metric is meant to serve, and whether the target is seeing the full label plus the full input or only part of it — awkawk's questions, never answered.

Exceptions for table labels, row and column headers together, and legends that sit far from their fields — raised by jake-abma citing mbgower's label-in-name issues. anevins12 asked in 2022 whether that meant spreadsheet-style grids or all tables and got no reply.
Whether this belongs in WCAG as a normative requirement at all, or in COGA design guidance or a separate best-practice document — raised by patrickhlauke and echoed by alastc.

mcking65's #890: whether the visual label and the programmatic name should be separate requirements, with the programmatic part moved into Roles, values, states, properties available. GreggVan disputed the proposed wording and asked for user outcomes to be listed first; no further discussion yet.
interactive-element-names-available.note: The activity is lopsided. 33 of the 34 comments sit on #194, and 30 of them were written in a two-week burst in March and April 2019; anevins12's 2022 question went unanswered and the thread was then dormant for four years until adampage revived it in May 2026. Of the issues that actually concern accessible names, tallneil's #93 and mraccess77's #184, itself a deferral from 2016, have never received a single reply, and mcking65's #890 from October 2026 has one, from GreggVan.

text-contrast-sufficient-minimum.headline: Whether the minimum test should be a contrast ratio at all, and whether a number computed from CSS colour values can predict whether rendered text is readable.

positions.label: Ratio is the wrong math
positions.detail: sdw32 says he was surprised to find the words "contrast ratio" still in the latest WCAG 3 draft, because there is neither empirical nor theoretical evidence that the eye perceives contrast in proportion to the lightest colour divided by the darkest; the evidence supports perception of a brightness difference, which is what APCA computes. He argues that for mobile devices in typical indoor lighting the eye adapts to the room, so the difference can be used directly without normalising against an average or ambient level, and points to his cedc.tools comparison of APCA against ratio for black and white text on coloured backgrounds. Myndex adds in #29 that 4.5:1 degrades the experience for 100% of sighted users rather than only impaired ones, that roughly 86% of sites fail WCAG 2 contrast on automated survey with some of those failures being perceptual artefacts rather than real inaccessibility, and offers a side-by-side dark-mode comparison in which the WCAG 2 minimum is unreadable while the APCA minimum is legible.

positions.label: The peer review has already happened
positions.detail: Issue #29 exists to answer the Contrast Subgroup's condition that APCA needs extensive peer review before adoption. Myndex's position is that peer review is not in the WCAG 3 charter and no other subgroup has been asked for it, and that APCA has been in open public beta since the stable February 2021 release regardless. The dossier lists journal and book-published work (Ulitin in Culture and Technologies Studies 2021 and a 2023 Springer chapter), Sam Waller's Cambridge paper "Does the contrast ratio actually predict the legibility of website text?", Chris Lilley's internal W3C review in the silver repo, and a Low Vision Task Force thread involving Bailey, Campbell and Avila. He renews a 2020 proposal that AGWG convene a standing panel of subject experts on the SMPTE or ISO model, on the grounds that it would strengthen the standard's footing in future legislation.

positions.label: Testable beats theoretically correct
positions.detail: GreggVan does not dispute that stroke weight, font design, presentation time and anti-aliasing all affect reading; he says stem width was considered and dropped because most people cannot measure it, and that the current simple measure is a deliberate trade, not an oversight. What he wants from critics is proposed wording: a single statement of the musts and a second of the shoulds, where a must is important, works across web technologies and has good interrater reliability. Machine testability is not required, only enough objectivity that different evaluators reach the same conclusion. He offers to have a "text visibility" tool built that takes font, size, type, stem and height and returns a linear score against a pass threshold, with a different threshold for running text than for menus, buttons and other short strings where the reader has time to fixate.

positions.label: A test without utility is worse than no test
positions.detail: Direct rebuttal to the testability framing in #266: if the result of the test lacks utility then making it testable has not helped, and because WCAG 2.x is now being written into law, a flawed test carries flawed consequences with it. He offers the APC-RC reference-font matching method as a simple testable alternative, where a designer matches their chosen typeface against reference fonts for the silver and gold levels, necessary because "normal" and "bold" mean substantially different things per family. He also disputes GreggVan's premise that authors will not handle multiple variables, saying designers work with x-height ratio and glyph weight routinely and prefer a range of options to a binary, and that in practice only the critical content text needs testing, body text above all, and only once.

positions.label: One threshold across all weights cannot work
positions.detail: sdw32's glance-readability study, about 40 participants shown random three and four letter words for 300 ms across Open Sans Light through Extra Bold at APCA Lc 30, 45, 60 and 75, found that the minimum workable font size depends on the interaction between weight and contrast: Open Sans Extra Bold at Lc 30 outperformed Open Sans Light at Lc 75. His proposed fix is to quantify weight by pixel density after Wilkins, rasterising sample text, cropping to the x-height and thresholding at RGB(128) to split the anti-aliased pixels; using Wilkins' "the quick brown fox" phrase that gives Open Sans Light 20.2%, Open Sans 30.7%, Open Sans Semibold 40.0%, Open Sans Bold 47.5%, Open Sans Extrabold 56.4%, with Arial 35.4% and Verdana Bold 50.3%. He later proposed switching to the bare alphabet so the method generalises beyond Latin, without publishing revised figures. TestPartners notes WCAG 2 recognises only 400 and 700 while weight 600 is common and reads as bold. patrickhlauke's objection is upstream of all of it: the same nominal CSS weight renders differently between typefaces and even between cuts of one typeface, so the value is meaningless unless anchored to specific font metrics, which font fallback then breaks.

positions.label: Nominal contrast is not rendered contrast
positions.detail: In #590 nakano0949-web proposes a rendering-aware model: a rendered glyph divides into a Core of pure glyph colour, an anti-aliased band of blended pixels, and a background ring, with Core Ratio approximated as (C/W) squared and AA Impact as 1 minus that. Measurements show AA impact climbing sharply below 14px and dominating at 12px and below, so text that passes on CSS colour values can measure substantially lower as actually drawn, worst for small sizes, thin weights and particular font cuts. The proposal supplies a five-step extraction algorithm to automate the measurement and offers data and code. patrickhlauke cross-references the earlier w3c/wcag#4954 discussion and elsewhere in #266 lists the same class of variables the model is trying to capture: OS anti-aliasing settings, font substitution, differing cuts, and the period when macOS rendered fonts visibly fatter than Windows in the same browser.

agreed: CSS colour values alone cannot reliably predict readability. nakano0949-web's Core/AA/BG-Ring model drew no rebuttal; Myndex replied only that the draft APC-RC considers anti-aliasing, without commenting on the model itself.

Font weight interacts with contrast. sdw32's glance data, which he says shows a simple contrast threshold for all font weights "is not fit for purpose", went unchallenged; GreggVan agreed weight and design matter but defended the current simple measure as a deliberate trade-off rather than conceding it is unfit.

Text size should be specified in device-independent CSS px rather than device pixels or anything measured on screen (patrickhlauke, Myndex, sdw32). Myndex gives the reference px as 0.0213 degrees or 1.278 minutes of arc, but also asked whether that value should be revised, since devices do not necessarily adhere to it.

Myndex's warning that WCAG 2's use of pt rather than px caused real-world error went unchallenged: designers apply the 3:1 large-text allowance at 18px when the breakpoint is 18pt, which is 24px, leaving the text 25% smaller than the standard intends.
open: Whether the minimum test stays a ratio. sdw32 raised it in #266; GreggVan's reply defended the simplicity of the current measure in general but nobody from the group addressed the ratio-versus-difference argument itself.

Whether WCAG 3 adopts a rendering-aware contrast measurement, which nakano0949-web says can be automated, or stays with nominal CSS colour values. nakano0949-web proposed it in #590 and only patrickhlauke and Myndex replied.

Whether APC-RC serves colour vision deficient and low vision users, which nakano0949-web put to Myndex directly. Myndex answered that APCA already improves on WCAG 2 for protans, that a protan compensator extension and the SACAM adjustable colour model are in progress, and that the silver and gold contrasts target a Pelli-Robson score down to 1, but those extensions are unreleased.

GreggVan's offer to have a text visibility tool built is conditional on someone supplying the research and the interaction data to define it. Myndex replied by pointing to the APC-RC reference-font matching method and a tool his group is developing, and sdw32 asked for comment on his pixel-density proposal; GreggVan has not responded to either.

Whether there is any minimum requirement on the default presentation of text at all, contrast included. sdw32 argues 200% or 500% zoom is worthless if the base rendering is already inadequate; GreggVan says no. The size half of that exchange is covered under text-style-readable-minimum.

Whether the definition of text being revised in #744, tied to human language, would let code shown to users, such as an HTML snippet, escape this contrast requirement. adampage raised it and no one has replied.
text-contrast-sufficient-minimum.note: Issue #29 is a standing evidence dossier rather than a discussion: opened in October 2023, reorganised in March 2025, last touched April 2026, and carrying no comments at all. sdw32's March 2026 objection in #266 tagged nine working group members by name (rachaelbradley, alastc, iadawn, giacomo-petri, julierawe, fstrr, MakotoUeki, hidde, GreggVan) and drew no reply in the thread; the only later comment is tsmd's note that x-height does not transfer to Japanese, Chinese or Korean.

user-settings-supported.headline: Whether an OS-level preference flag such as prefers-reduced-motion is a strong enough signal to hang a normative requirement on, or too blunt an instrument to build one from — an argument fought out in 2020 that has barely moved since.

positions.label: The preference is the requirement
positions.detail: CharlesBelov's original ask (#183) was that where the OS exposes the request and the user agent passes it to content, not animating should satisfy AA — the user telling their OS that animation is problematic removes the need for anyone to decide whether a given animation is problematic. guyhickling points out that Android's "Remove animations", iOS's "Reduce motion" and Windows 10's "Show animations" are all binary switches that set the same flag, and that honouring it costs an author a media query rather than banning animation, with an opt-in button available where the animation is genuinely informational. mgifford and guyhickling both argue AAA is where requirements go to be ignored, because AA is the norm most IT teams work to. CharlesBelov later adds that the need goes beyond VIMS to hyper-vigilance and attention impairments, where even small, sub-second animation costs focus, and asks to be believed that an OS-level request is sufficient without waiting for a study.

positions.label: A binary flag is not a mandate
positions.detail: prefers-reduced-motion is one bit, but users are affected by specific magnitudes and kinds of motion, so reading it as "no animation at all" would technically fail a page containing a single dot that fades by one opacity value. He cites Windows users who set the preference accidentally without realising what it does. His counter-proposal, building on mgifford's #182 suggestion that respecting user choices such as dark mode be at least AAA, is a generic "respect user settings" requirement at AAA covering dark mode, reduced motion and high contrast, phrased in Understanding rather than hard-coded to whichever media queries exist today, with honouring a preference offered as a sufficient technique rather than the normative bar — and even then subject to whether it is accessibility supported.

positions.label: Define the threshold and show the evidence first
positions.detail: Specifying size across devices and zoom levels, and duration when the motion is triggered by user action such as scrolling, is exactly where this stalled during WCAG 2.1. Small animations such as icons changing on hover did not appear to be vestibular triggers, so a minimum size looks necessary before the requirement can sit at A or AA. The preference is not a 1:1 fit for the user need, so relying on it produces false positives and extra work; in a consensus process that means persuading the people who objected last time. Answering CharlesBelov's invocation of the W3C Code of Conduct, he redirects to the priority-levels wiki as the document that actually governs level decisions.

positions.label: The platform plumbing does not work yet
positions.detail: JAWS-test's cross-browser test of prefers-color-scheme (#182) found Edge reporting light even in Dark Mode and dark only under high contrast white-on-black, Firefox reporting light even in HCM, Chrome mapping some HCM modes to dark and others to no-preference, Android Chrome always reporting light even in Dark Mode, and only iOS Safari behaving as expected. mraccess77 reports the Windows setting blocks animations they want along with those they do not, and asks for finer control. MarjaE2 (#40) found user CSS forcing animation-timing-function and transition-timing-function to step-start is overridden by ::before and ::after pseudo-elements carrying their own timing functions, and argues disabled users should not have to become programmers to browse without being hurt. Myndex challenges the CSS Color Adjust rule that maps Canvas lightness (L below 33% or above 67%) onto prefers-color-scheme, on the grounds that CIELAB L is not perceptually uniform on self-illuminated displays and the real flip point is higher.

positions.label: Scope the settings list, and say what respecting means
positions.detail: COGA (#737, filed by julierawe) wants haptics added to the note that currently lists font size, icon size, color scheme, magnification and motion, or the list reworded as "include but are not limited to", and asks whether the separate Haptic stimulation adjustable provision in the Animation section is still needed once haptics is covered here. JAWS-test asked the foundational question in 2020 — what does respecting a preference actually oblige an author to do, should pages invert, and what about a page already rendered light-on-dark. mgifford adds two cases nobody answered: dark mode can switch with the time of day so the preference changes mid-session without the user doing anything, and an on-page theme widget should take precedence over the browser preference.

agreed: Some requirement to respect user preferences should exist; nobody argued it should not. mgifford proposed in #182 that respecting user choices such as dark mode be at least AAA, patrickhlauke agreed and generalised it to a technology-neutral "respect user settings/preferences" requirement, and alastc suggested an SC centered around the preference might be a better approach. Whether that generic shape beats a dedicated criterion is not agreed: guyhickling and CharlesBelov wanted a motion-specific requirement at AA.
Respect runs both ways: a site that is dark by default is not honouring a user who has asked for prefers-color-scheme: light. patrickhlauke's point, unrebutted.

Support for these preferences is inconsistent enough across browsers and platforms that any requirement has to be conditioned on environments that support it — JAWS-test's test results went unchallenged, with patrickhlauke cautioning only that dark mode and high contrast mode are distinct things that correlate.
open: What "respecting" a preference concretely obliges an author to do. JAWS-test asked in 2020 and got only patrickhlauke's "taking the cue from the user's preference request and actually doing something about it" — no testable formulation followed.
Whether haptics belongs in the note, and whether Haptic stimulation adjustable can then be removed from the Animation section. Raised by julierawe for the COGA Task Force in #737; no replies.
Whether the note's list of accessibility-related user settings is closed or illustrative (julierawe).
How to indicate to the user when an on-site theme control diverges from their browser preference (mgifford).

Whether user-side remedies are good enough that the requirement is unnecessary. CharlesBelov's own assessment against the priority-levels wiki was "a big Maybe": his user stylesheet sets animation-duration and transition-duration to 0 but does nothing for animated GIFs or JavaScript animation, and the only Firefox extension he found was outside Mozilla's security review.
Whether ::before and ::after overriding user CSS is a WCAG matter at all or a CSS specification defect. MarjaE2 raised it in #40 and was not sure where to report it.

Whether size and duration thresholds are the route forward (mgifford's sketch of a quantity-of-movement metric, answered by patrickhlauke's screen-rulers-and-calculators objection, to which mgifford replied that the contrast ratios once looked equally arbitrary until tools made them easy to evaluate), or whether the preference alone suffices.

How strong the case is that dark mode is a need rather than a stylistic choice. mgifford said some people need it to see text effectively, avoid headaches or focus; patrickhlauke's cited study found some benefit for users with cloudy ocular media but no overall impact on what was measured.
user-settings-supported.note: Three of the four threads carry almost no discussion. #40 was closed without a single reply, #737 has had no response since COGA filed it in June 2026, and #182 went quiet after 2020 until one technical comment from Myndex in 2025. Effectively the whole argument lives in #183, which is dual-labelled with No visual motion and whose substance dates from 2020, with one 2025 comment from MarjaE2 reporting that drastic animation — autoplaying video, marquee text, elements that bounce or strobe once a user substitutes their own fonts — remains common, including on the W3C's own WCAG 3 introduction page.

text-contrast-sufficient-enhanced.headline: Whether a higher contrast threshold buys anything once text is past contrast constancy, and how a higher tier would relate to thresholds keyed to what the text is for.

positions.label: Above contrast constancy, more contrast is the wrong lever
positions.detail: Myndex rests his argument on Lovie-Kitchin's critical contrast, the point past which further increases in text-to-background contrast produce no improvement in reading speed or comprehension. Once a design reaches that Lc level it enters contrast constancy, and from there the spatial factors — whitespace, stroke weight, size, crowding — govern readability, with the perceived luminance difference ranking, in his words, among the least important. He cites Chung and Tjan for the mechanism: reading speed shows strong spatial-frequency dependence when text contrast is low, which is to say the payoff from added contrast is conditional on size and weight rather than additive to them. sdw32's glance study, which tested APCA Lc 30, 45, 60 and 75, supplies a matching data point, with Open Sans Extra Bold at APCA Lc 30 outperforming Open Sans Light at Lc 75, from which he concludes a single contrast threshold for all font weights is not fit for purpose (the weight-quantification method behind it is covered under text-contrast-sufficient-minimum).

positions.label: Key the requirement to a use-case taxonomy
positions.detail: Myndex's #207 restructure groups 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) and 1.4.6 Contrast (Enhanced) under one guideline, "Visually readable content uses ample luminance contrast," keeping 1.4.6 as its own row and attaching to it 1.4.6a on font weight and glyph characteristics and 1.4.6b on text use cases. His categories are FLUENT — high-fluent body text, defined as more than two continuous lines in a block or column at an x-height of about 16px or less, fluent text up to two and a half lines, and large fluent headers above about 32px — and SUB-FLUENT, covering soft readability, spot readability (readable with fixation), logo and branding colours, and incidental text in images. GreggVan, in #266 and without reference to the enhanced level, proposes a text visibility tool with one pass threshold X for running text and a different X for menus, buttons and other short strings where the reader has time to fixate.

positions.label: Magnification covers low vision, so no size floor
positions.detail: Answering sdw32's question about minimum size and contrast requirements for default presentation, GreggVan's position is that if a size is large enough for typical vision, then that size under magnification is good enough for low vision — large print for typical viewers is large print for low vision users, fine print is fine print, and anyone with very low vision has magnification built into every OS. He adds that stating any floor would require specifying screen size and CSS pitch, which the author does not control, and says a lot of thought went into concluding there is no way to guarantee text is never too small.

positions.label: Zoom has a ceiling, so a size floor has to be in the default
positions.detail: sdw32 rejects the premise of typical vision outright — vision is a bell curve like grip strength, and he routinely measures young people at 20/10, twice the 20/20 reference. Since designers default to designing for themselves, a site built by a 20/10 designer accommodates only 20/50 at the browser maximum of 500% zoom, which he does not accept as maximising foreseeable use. Working backwards from 20/200 access at 500% gives a target of 20/40 suitability at 100%, which is his 8 CSS px x-height floor. On GreggVan's pitch objection he answers that no screen pitch need be specified, only the CSS px definition itself — 96 DPI viewed at 28 inches or 711mm, implying 427mm for a 160 DPI phone — and offers a live failure, the string "achetés = 30% d'économies" on carrefour.fr, as text that fails EN 301 549 while passing the current WCAG 3 draft. The minimum-level half of this exchange is covered under text-contrast-sufficient-minimum and text-style-readable-minimum.

positions.label: The real enhanced requirement is triggered by circumstance, not by tier
positions.detail: EN 301 549 v4.1.0, which sdw32 worked on, already ships the two-level structure but keys it to whether the text can be enlarged rather than to a conformance level. Zoomable text gets a best-practice x-height of at least 8 CSS px, corresponding to 1.2mm at a 400mm viewing distance with no zooming or screen scaling; text and images of text necessary for all functionality that is closed to text enlargement get at least 16 CSS px of x-height, an exact doubling. The weight rule he wrote for the separate non-digital standard interpreting the European Accessibility Act is two-sided rather than a floor: body text between regular-weight and semi-bold Open Sans, and keywords or short phrases neither thinner than regular Open Sans nor heavier than extra-bold.

positions.label: The gold level is defined by a clinical target, not by a multiple
positions.detail: APC-RC carries silver and gold levels with reference fonts a designer matches their own typeface against, and Myndex states the selected contrasts for both are intended to serve a Pelli-Robson score down to 1, a profound contrast deficit on a scale where 2 is normal and lower is worse. That makes the higher tier an answer to a measured population rather than a round multiple of the minimum. nakano0949-web pressed him in #590 on whether APC-RC addresses colour vision deficiency and low vision, which she said physical contrast models alone cannot fully capture; Myndex answered that APCA already improves on WCAG 2 for protans, that a protan compensator pre-shaping luminances for colours with high red primary content is due this year, and that SACAM, an accessibility-adjustable colour model for dynamic personalisation, is in progress. In #207 he notes the same physics already rejects pure red against black or dark colours, since red on black is poor for standard vision too.

agreed: Luminance contrast and the spatial properties of text are not independent levers. Myndex's framing that contrast sensitivity is dictated by spatial frequency, which he calls peer-reviewed consensus dating to Stevens 1961 and Bartleson and Breneman 1967, drew no rebuttal in either thread where he raised it.

Not everything in a view should be at maximum contrast or maximum size. Myndex argues variation is required for visual hierarchy and for cognitive accessibility in particular, and GreggVan's separate thresholds for running text and for short strings reach the same conclusion from the testability side.

Whatever the enhanced requirement asks for has to be anchored in x-height rather than font-size. sdw32 states he absolutely agrees with Myndex on this; the ratios that make font-size uninstructive are 0.55 for Verdana, 0.52 for Arial and Helvetica and 0.45 for Times New Roman. teohhanhui's correction that CSS already has the ex unit was answered by Myndex — ex is a length unit, not a way to set rendered glyph size, which is what the font-x-size proposal in csswg-drafts#6709 exists for — and teohhanhui did not press it. tsmd later cautioned that x-height does not directly apply to Japanese, Chinese or Korean.
open: Whether a separate enhanced level should exist at all. No participant argues against it; Myndex's #207 keeps 1.4.6 Contrast (Enhanced) as a row with font-weight and text-use-case sub-items, and has sat since February 2023 with no comment from anyone.

What the enhanced threshold actually is. No participant in any of the three threads proposes or defends a numeric value for it. sdw32's Lc 30, 45, 60 and 75 are study conditions rather than proposals, and APC-RC's gold level is named but never given a value.

alastc's requirement list in #266 opens with "Maximum text contrast: The rendered text against its background meets a maximum ‘contrast ratio test’ for its text appearance." and no one in the thread's twenty-plus comments addressed the maximum. Myndex's argument against uniform maximum contrast bears on it but never names it.

Whether an enhanced threshold stated in CSS colour values survives rendering at the sizes where it matters. nakano0949-web's measurements in #590 show anti-aliasing impact climbing sharply below 14px and dominating at 12px and below; only patrickhlauke and Myndex replied.
Whether the protan compensator and SACAM change the enhanced-level answer once released. Both were described as forthcoming in April 2026 and the thread records no release.

sdw32's pixel-density method for quantifying font weight was put to the group with three explicit questions — is everyone happy with the approach, does a public-domain algorithm exist, and will anyone reimplement it outside VBA to check his numbers. He asked on 20 January 2026 and re-asked on 10 February tagging Myndex and GreggVan by name. Neither answered.

Whether any of this transfers beyond Latin scripts. tsmd's closing comment in #266 is that x-height does not directly apply to Japanese, Chinese or Korean; Myndex's own note that Japanese mixes thin-stroked logographic Kanji with thicker syllabic Kana on the same line means a single spatial threshold is already strained within one writing system.

How far text zoom must go. Myndex says 200% only reaches accommodation for 20/40 and body text should be able to reach 400%, 16px to 64px and 48px headlines to 96px-128px, with diminishing returns beyond about 2 degrees; sdw32 reasons from the 500% browser maximum, and GreggVan relies on AT magnification as much as is needed. No one engaged Myndex's figures directly.
text-contrast-sufficient-enhanced.note: There is no discussion specific to the enhanced level. All three threads carry both the minimum and enhanced provision labels, and every substantive exchange in them is about the floor — whether a minimum exists, what unit it uses, how weight is quantified. #207, the only thread that engages the enhanced level structurally, was opened by Myndex in February 2023 as a survey item, was last updated in May 2026, carries six provision labels including graphical object, interactive element, focus indicator and pointer contrast, and has never received a single comment.

text-style-readable-enhanced.headline: Nobody has said what the enhanced level actually raises — the two threads specific to this provision have no replies, and the shared requirements thread is arguing about whether a second, stricter threshold can be defined at all now that the baseline it would sit above has been removed.

positions.label: One scale, two cut-offs
positions.detail: Rather than write separate prose for each level, build a text visibility tool that takes font, size, type, stem and height into account and returns a linear research-based score; point it at any text and pass above X. Proposes a different X for running text, which the eye must read at speed as it passes over the line, than for menus, buttons and other short strings where the user dwells on a word. He did not address the enhanced level as such; on this approach enhanced would be a higher number on the same scale. He offers to have the tool built — but only if someone supplies the research and the interaction effects, which he asked sdw32 for directly.

positions.label: Tier by reference font, not by number
positions.detail: Because font-size and the labels normal and bold mean substantially different things across families, the APC-RC guidelines set silver and gold levels using reference fonts that a designer matches their own typeface against, a one-time exercise per font. His acuity-reserve table, which does not mention an enhanced level, runs in small steps: 0.18 degrees, an 8.3px x-height or a 16px font at Helvetica's 0.52 ratio, is content minimum at critical size, 0.2 degrees (9.4px x-height, 18px font) is the figure for columns and blocks, and 0.24 degrees (11px x-height, 21.5px font) is preferred body. He also insists a practical standard must not demand that everything in a view hit critical values, since spot text such as a copyright bug and sub-fluent text such as captions exist deliberately to keep the visual hierarchy readable.

positions.label: Tier by what the user cannot zoom
positions.detail: He points to EN 301 549, which has a two-level shape: an 8 CSS px x-height as best practice for text that can be zoomed, against a 16 CSS px x-height for text and images of text necessary for functionality that is closed to text enlargement. His glance-readability study — roughly 40 participants, random three- and four-letter words at 300 ms, across Open Sans Light through Extra Bold and APCA 30 to 75 — found Open Sans Extra Bold at APCA 30 outperforming Open Sans Light at APCA 75, so the minimum appropriate font size depends on the interaction of weight and APCA contrast, and a single contrast threshold applied across all weights is not fit for purpose. For weight he proposes Wilkins' pixel-density measure (rasterise the alphabet, crop to the x-height, threshold at RGB 128, count black pixels), giving Open Sans Light 20.2 percent, regular 30.7, semibold 40.0, bold 47.5 and extrabold 56.4 — which would turn the regular-to-semibold Open Sans body-text band, from text he wrote for the non-digital standard interpreting the European Accessibility Act, into a testable range.

positions.label: A narrower band has less room for rendering error
positions.detail: patrickhlauke lists the rendering variation that makes nominal size and weight values unreliable to test: OS antialiasing, font fallback and substitution, different cuts of the same typeface with subtly different metrics, and browser rendering that made fonts on macOS visually fatter than on Windows. scottaohara adds that CSS scaling can change the rendered size while the specified font-size stays exactly as authored, so the declared value is not the tested value. TestPartners notes that weight 600 is very common and looks bold while strictly not being bold, so any level that keeps the binary normal/bold split has to say how intermediate values are treated. patrickhlauke supports building GreggVan's tool but treats these as the caveats it must carry.

positions.label: Replace the prohibitions with a user preference
positions.detail: The enhanced level is currently stricter by banning things — no underlining, no decorative or cursive face. In #266 detlevhfischer called the decorative-or-cursive wording too restrictive as a general rule, and Myndex agreed and called it subjective, ambiguous and arbitrary (the same objection recorded against the minimum); neither commented on underlining, and detlevhfischer did not comment on the alternative. Myndex's counter-proposal reshapes what enhanced would mean: require that a plain accessible font is offered as a fallback and that layout features keep working when the user selects it, ideally through a new prefers-font-family: plain media query. The argument is that a stricter author prohibition is the wrong instrument for a dynamic medium where user personalisation can do the work, especially as these voluntary guidelines are being pressed into law.

positions.label: The stricter rule belongs at minimum
positions.detail: In #641, a voice recognition software user points out the asymmetry directly: the minimum permits some underlining and the enhanced requirement does not. Having repeatedly tried to open a link that turned out to be randomly underlined text, they want underlining restricted to links at the minimum level — which would collapse the distinction between the two levels on this point rather than preserve it. They argue underlining is a holdover from handwriting, and that digital text has bold and italic for emphasis while underlining has become the convention for links.

agreed: x-height, not CSS font-size, is the right anchor for any size threshold. sdw32 states he absolutely agrees with Myndex on this and notes deriving x-height for a given font is fairly trivial programmatically if you hold the licence; teohhanhui's observation that CSS already has the ex length unit was answered — it measures length but cannot set the rasterised size on screen — and the gap is the proposed font-x-size property (csswg-drafts #6709). Nobody argued for keeping font-size as the anchor. tsmd later questioned whether x-height applies at all to Japanese, Chinese and Korean (see open).
