Running text and short strings need different thresholds. GreggVan reaches this from how the text is read (you dwell on a button label, you skim a line of body text) and Myndex from readability science (spot and sub-fluent text are legitimate design), and neither was contested.

Any absolute size in the spec should be given primarily in CSS px with pt secondary. Myndex's worked example went unrebutted: WCAG 2 specifies 18pt, designers apply the number as 18px, and the resulting text is 25 percent smaller than the standard requires.
open: What the enhanced requirement is for at all. julierawe asked in #484 whether it simply encourages developers to set default text presentation to the values already specified in the foundational adjustable text style requirement, how that connection could be made clearer, and whether that framing means customisation beyond those values is no longer encouraged. The issue has had no replies since December 2025, and she noted that commenters raised similar questions about readable blocks of text enhanced (#485).

What the enhanced numbers are. The candidates on the table have never been compared: sdw32's 16 CSS px x-height for text closed to enlargement against his 8 CSS px baseline, versus Myndex's ladder from 0.18 degrees (16px font) to 0.24 degrees (21.5px font).
Whether underlining should be forbidden at enhanced only or at both levels — Finnberrys (#641), unanswered since April 2026.

Whether sdw32's pixel-density approach to font weight is sound. He asked three explicit questions — is the approach acceptable, does a free public-domain algorithm exist that could run in a website, will anyone reimplement his VBA to check his numbers — and pinged Myndex and GreggVan by name in February 2026. None has been answered.
Whether the research exists to build GreggVan's scale. He asked for the interactions; sdw32 offered his experimental data and asked to join meetings; nothing has been assembled.

Whether a scored tool that returns one number is preferable to asking authors to work with several text characteristics. GreggVan said anything requiring an author to look up several characteristics and their interactions would not be practical, and patrickhlauke endorsed the tool with rendering caveats; Myndex disagreed, saying designers are more interested in working with a range of options than arbitrary binary choices, that they already refer to x-height ratio and glyph weight all the time, and that a testable result lacking utility is not helpful.

Whether an enhanced tier can be specified above a floor that was removed. GreggVan confirmed there is no longer a minimum size requirement for default text presentation and sdw32 registered deep concern; the argument is recorded in full against the minimum entry, and nobody in the thread drew out what it means for the enhanced level.

tsmd's point that x-height does not apply to Japanese, Chinese or Korean, which every size proposal here depends on. Earlier, in February 2026, sdw32 had replaced Wilkins' English pangram with the plain alphabet for his density metric so that it would generalise to other alphabets, but that is still a Latin-script fix, and no one has responded to tsmd.
text-style-readable-enhanced.note: Both issues specific to this provision — #484 and #641 — have zero comments, so everything substantive here is drawn from #266, a requirements-tracking thread shared with the minimum level and both text contrast provisions. Part of the record is also off-thread: sdw32 posted his central proposal as a .docx attachment because the GitHub editor does not support the lists and images he needed, and, on the thread, separately asked GreggVan for the basic process rules — whether must and should apply, whether tests have to be machine-executable, and what the deadlines are — which GreggVan answered by saying the group does not use must and should, that anything treated as a must needs to be important, reliably testable with good interrater reliability and work across web technologies, and that it can be human-testable as long as it is objective enough that evaluators reach the same conclusion.

image-alternatives-available.headline: Whether "available" means available to everyone or only through assistive technology, and whether "equivalent" is a definition problem the standard can fix or a practice problem it cannot.

positions.label: Available should mean visible, not just programmatic
positions.detail: MarcHaunschild opened #191 arguing there is no icon everyone understands, and that an aria-label serves only screen reader users — the sighted majority, people who do not read the Latin alphabet, and speech-input users get nothing. His example is the GitHub editor toolbar, where a large A beside a small A could equally mean resize text; it actually means add header text, and he says he would never have guessed. He reports Germany's BITV-Test once required textual descriptions for icons and dropped the requirement to align with WCAG, which he treats as a regression. alastc drafted the requirement as "a visible text equivalent for icons is available" with icon defined as a non-text representation of a function or discrete piece of information, such as a printer for print or a green tick for complete; MarcHaunschild accepted it and asked for a carve-out, "unless it is essential to be without text", for cases such as a game where guessing the shape is the point.

positions.label: It was tried and no mechanism survived touch
positions.detail: alastc reported in March 2020 that DavidMacDonald's proposal was worked through in the group and put to a member survey, and that coverage broke down across four scenarios: active and inactive icons, on mouse and on touchscreen. A hover tooltip handles the mouse cases cleanly, but on a touchscreen the user cannot reach the text without activating the control or relying on a flaky double tap, and forcing visible labels into a toolbar destroys the toolbar's purpose. LJWatson cautioned separately against title attributes and the SVG title element becoming the recommended route, since those tooltips are not dismissable; awkawk noted 1.4.13's exception for user-agent-controlled presentation makes them technically permissible, and LJWatson accepted the exemption while maintaining the practice should not be encouraged. detlevhfischer pushed back on the related proposal to extend Label in Name to graphical buttons, asking what a speech-input user would actually say — "click i", "click italics" — and pointing to the existing symbolic-text-characters exception as the right answer.

positions.label: Equivalence has collapsed into a compliance formality
positions.detail: His #370 argument is that "equivalent" has been so weakly defined that a file name passes in practice: "dog32234.jpg" tells you nothing about breed, setting, activity or the rhetorical reason the image was chosen, and he demonstrates the gap by asking whether readers pictured a French Bulldog on a Hawaiian beach or a Rottweiler on a grassy field. He cites Perkins at under 1 percent of the web compliant, AudioEye at roughly 3 percent and WebAIM at 4 percent, and argues Instagram's billion-plus uploads a day are being pushed toward GenAI descriptions of the form "Might be a man, wearing glasses". He wants equivalence defined against the academic literature on information exchange and extended explicitly to maps, charts, tables, data visualizations and descriptions of people, rather than a title plus a one-sentence overview. In #371 he makes the parallel terminology case: "image" excludes maps, charts and data visualizations in most people's minds, and WCAG should adopt static Audio Description, the term used by the American Council of the Blind, the American Foundation for the Blind, RNIB, the World Blind Union, the American Alliance of Museums and the US National Park Service, over image description, which is largely a computer-science coinage.

positions.label: The requirement is sound; the ecosystem is not
positions.detail: patrickhlauke's first reply is a flat correction: "dog32234.jpg" does not pass, it fails 1.1.1 as an inappropriate text alternative. TestPartners argues authors misusing text alternatives is not a loophole — testers frequently do not test the criterion correctly, automated tools cannot yet judge appropriateness, and the root causes are education and authoring platforms that do not help; WCAG 3 cannot and will not fix that. brett-oppegaard called that a defeatist attitude and proposed that WCAG 3 tighten its definitions, add more scaffolding, and create more metrics and benchmarks to close the gap between intent and practice. He adds a newer structural cause: organizations now store images in digital asset management systems with the alt text attached, so the text is written with no knowledge of the context it will be used in, which is why it defaults to a literal description of the image contents. yatil makes the division-of-labour point — W3C defines conformance, laws enforce it, and under the European Accessibility Act member states must stand up agencies with fines behind EN 301 549's reference to WCAG 2.1.

positions.label: Equivalence is the wrong goal to aim at
positions.detail: In #272 he asks the group to revisit his proposal "Meaningful images have a text alternative" in place of the current goal that users have equivalent alternatives. His grounds are that decades of evidence show equivalence at scale does not work — he cites WebAIM's finding that nearly a third of images on popular home pages have missing, questionable or repetitive alternative text — and that even where alt text exists there is no agreement on what an equivalent is: ask ten experts and you get ten answers, with far wider spread in the wild. He frames the fix as inter-rater reliability, pointing to slides he presented to the working group three years earlier, and argues a meaningfulness test is both more scalable now and better positioned for changes in technology.

positions.label: Equivalent to what, exactly
positions.detail: #499 takes the draft sentence on its own terms: "Equivalent text alternatives are available for images that convey content" does not say what the alternative must be equivalent to. He notes that someone carrying WCAG 2 knowledge assumes the intent is the purpose of the image, but read cold the wording points at the content of the image instead — under which "House icon" would be correct and "home" would not.

agreed: The state of alt text in the wild is poor. brett-oppegaard and mbgower cite overlapping evidence for it and TestPartners does not dispute it; they differ on whether the standard is implicated in the cause.

patrickhlauke's correction that a file-name alt already fails WCAG 2.x 1.1.1 was echoed by yatil and TestPartners. brett-oppegaard did not dispute the normative reading but maintained that file names and one-line alt text are what he finds in practice, and turned to enforcement and interpretation.

yatil's account of where the buck stops — W3C sets the standard, civil rights law and the EAA enforce it, and W3C has neither budget nor intent to review billions of sites — was accepted by brett-oppegaard, who redirected to the DOJ Title II rule.

TestPartners' digital-asset-management argument is unrebutted and brett-oppegaard endorsed the underlying problem, agreeing descriptions should be crafted per use and logged so a recontextualization trail exists, while conceding that would require a major shift in archiving practice.
Nobody defended the title attribute or the SVG title element as the technique to recommend, even after awkawk established it is permissible under 1.4.13's user-agent exception.
open: Whether a visible text equivalent for icons should be required at all. MarcHaunschild's #191 has had no substantive comment since alastc reported the survey outcome in March 2020, and no one has proposed a touchscreen mechanism since.
Whether "equivalent" is measured against the image's content or its purpose. WilcoFiers raised it in #499 in January 2026 and the issue has no replies.

Whether the provision must say something specific about maps, charts, tables and data visualizations rather than treating them as images. brett-oppegaard asked for it in #370 and it was not taken up in a thread that turned to enforcement instead.

Whether "image" and "alt text" should be retired in favour of static Audio Description. brett-oppegaard's #371 has been open since September 2025 with zero comments, so the terminology argument the decorative-images threads defer to here has in fact never been answered.
Whether mbgower's meaningfulness framing replaces the equivalence goal. He asked twice in July 2025 and offered to walk the group through it; no one has responded on the issue.

Whether WCAG should say anything about over-specifying attributes in a description. rusteinberg's #251 raises the risk of an author writing "African American man working on his computer" about someone who is neither, and suggests "Man working on his computer" instead; MakotoUeki, then the Alt Text subgroup lead, asked which writing guide the advice came from in November 2021 and the thread stopped there.

MarcHaunschild's "unless it is essential to be without text" exception, and detlevhfischer's question of what a speech-input user would say for a graphical button, were both raised once and never examined.
image-alternatives-available.note: This provision is discussed far less than its filing count suggests: 7 threads and 23 comments, of which #191 (11) and #370 (8) account for most of the exchange and three others (#251, #371, #499) are effectively unanswered. #191 predates WCAG 3's provision structure by six years, and the substantive record for it — the acceptance survey alastc worked from — sits behind a W3C member-only link, so the reasoning for dropping the icon requirement is not publicly readable here. sydneycolemanfromgoogle's #518, on the decorative versus purely decorative distinction, is labelled against this provision but adampage marked it as a duplicate of #466 (it remains open), which moves that whole argument into the decorative-images-hidden record. As there, brett-oppegaard participates by email, so his comments arrive with quoted reply chains attached.

captions-available-prerecorded.headline: Only one real argument happened here — whether open captions are images of text — and it was settled; the rest of the provision is unanswered proposals, including the request to define "important sounds", which drew no replies at all.

positions.label: Open captions are images of text
positions.detail: Argued in #23 that open captions are literally pixels of text burned into video frames, so they would fail 1.4.5 Images of Text at AA if they had alt text, and otherwise fail 1.1.1 Non-text Content at A, since no video frame carries alt text. Conceded awkawk's rebuttal on the alt-text point but held the substantive request: open-captioned video should be required to carry a textual transcript in WCAG 3, not only from 1.2.8 upward. Raised the edge case of instructional video with music-only audio, where the captions are effectively carrying video-only time-based media.

positions.label: Open captions already conform
positions.detail: Open captions are part of the time-based media, not separate non-text content, so the alternative required at Level A is the alternative for the video as a whole. Captions of either kind are equivalents for audio information, so the Prerecorded Video-Only provision u9000-Nine cited does not apply — video-only content has no audio and therefore no captions. Stated flatly that open captions pass Level A, full stop, and that a transcript for audio information is not required until 1.2.8.

positions.label: Speaker identification should be required
positions.detail: Argues in #23 that without knowing who said what, a story or issue becomes hard to follow, and that this is critical for people with face-blindness — Finnberrys identifies people by voice, so muted or inaccessible audio removes the only cue. Compares captions without speaker identification to reading a playscript with no character names, and cites Teams meetings, where visible names do the work that in-person recognition cannot. Makes the same case for blind users reading captions or a transcript on a braille display.

positions.label: Speaker identification is more contingent than that
positions.detail: u9000-Nine notes that identifying speakers by caption position on screen does nothing for someone with face-blindness, since the cue still depends on matching a location to a face. mitchellevan calls the discussion North-America-centric for assuming the identifier is text, pointing to the BBC's subtitle guidance recommending colour to distinguish speakers, a practice also common in continental Europe — while acknowledging colour identification may itself fail Use of Color. Neither rejects the need; both points bear on which mechanism would satisfy it, and mitchellevan asks for more international context.

positions.label: Exemptions belong to regulators, not the standard
positions.detail: On whether advertising and promotional video should carry less weight than primary content, mraccess77 points out that inaccessible video causes clear discrimination in areas such as fair housing and healthcare, and draws the parallel to audio description, once dismissed as unnecessary for entertainment until entertainment was recognised as a right too. mitchellevan agrees on equal weight: user needs and technical feasibility are the same, "promotional" resists definition, and regulations such as the US Air Carrier Access Act already carve out advertising where a jurisdiction wants that. Prioritisation should sit in regulation, not be baked into a technical standard.

positions.label: Captions alone do not give Deaf users access
positions.detail: InfoGapBuster, writing as a Deaf person in #325, argues auto-generated subtitles may be inaccurate or fail to convey tone and nuance, and that WCAG 2.0 putting sign language at AAA led to limited implementation. Cites 250,000 to 500,000 primary ASL users in the US per Gallaudet, roughly 70 million Deaf people globally per the World Federation of the Deaf, about 60,000 JSL users in Japan, and 90 to 97 percent of Deaf children born to hearing parents with the resulting risk of language deprivation. Wants sign language translation — prepared in advance, distinct from live interpretation — named as a distinct outcome, arguing that requiring it would generate demand, grow the interpreter pool and accumulate training data. md84419 goes further, calling for a sign language alternative to website text and citing the BSL Act 2022, the Equality Act 2010, the Irish Sign Language Act 2017, the Korean Sign Language Act 2016 and the New Zealand Sign Language Act 2006 as evidence that language-based discrimination is already legally constrained.

agreed: Advertising and promotional video should carry the same weight as primary content in the standard itself, with any exemption left to regulators — mraccess77 and mitchellevan, unrebutted.

awkawk's reading that open captions are part of the time-based media and need no alternative text of their own was accepted by u9000-Nine ("That is fair"), narrowing the dispute to whether a transcript should also be required.
GreggVan's procedural point that no conformance level has been finalised, so nothing definitive can be said about what Bronze, Silver or Gold require, went unchallenged.
open: What counts as an "important sound". sydneycolemanfromgoogle opened #525 arguing the term is subjective and leads to missing context; the issue has no replies.
Whether open-captioned video must also provide a textual transcript in WCAG 3 — u9000-Nine's core request in #23, which awkawk acknowledged as clear but did not agree or disagree with.
Whether speaker identification is required, and whether text, colour or caption position satisfies it — raised by Finnberrys, complicated by u9000-Nine and mitchellevan.

Whether closed captions should be preferred over open captions, or open captions barred on new material, and how caption accuracy is graded across missing words, missing audio cues, absent speaker labels and punctuation carrying emphasis or sarcasm — all posed in WilcoFiers's original #23 body and none answered.
Whether MakotoUeki's proposal in #463 to merge other prerecorded-caption requirements into this one is accepted; the issue, opened in December 2025, has drawn no comments.

Whether the sign-language material belongs under this provision at all. md84419 argues in #325 that what is being discussed is text alternatives and needs a new section in 2.2 Text and Wording rather than 2.1 Image and Media Alternatives.
captions-available-prerecorded.note: Thin and asynchronous. Nineteen comments across four issues, two of which (#463 and #525) have zero replies, and the substantive exchange in #23 ran from September to November 2023, with two follow-up comments from mitchellevan a year later. InfoGapBuster's own proposed tiering permits auto-generated captions at Bronze, which sits awkwardly against the same comment's argument that automatic subtitles are unreliable — nobody in the thread picked this up.
